paragraphs: Beside a great forest lived a poor woodcutter with his wife and two children. The boy was called Hansel and the girl Grethel. He had little enough to eat, and when a great famine struck the land, he could no longer find even their daily bread. One night he lay tossing anxiously in bed, thinking about this. He groaned and said to his wife, “What will become of us? How can we feed our poor children when we have nothing left even for ourselves?” “I’ll tell you what, husband,” the woman answered. “Early tomorrow morning, we’ll take the children into the thickest part of the forest. We’ll light them a fire and give each one another piece of bread. Then we’ll go to work and leave them alone. They won’t find their way home, and we’ll be rid of them.” “No, wife,” the man said. “I won’t do that. How could I bear to leave my children alone in the forest? Wild animals would soon come and tear them to pieces.” “Oh, you fool!” she said. “Then all four of us must starve. You might as well plane the boards for our coffins.” She gave him no peace until he agreed. “All the same, I feel very sorry for the poor children,” he said.

The two children had also been unable to sleep because they were hungry, and they heard what their stepmother said to their father. Grethel wept bitterly. “Now we’re done for,” she told Hansel. “Hush, Grethel,” Hansel said. “Don’t upset yourself. I’ll soon find a way to help us.” Once the grown-ups were asleep, he got up, put on his little coat, opened the downstairs door and slipped outside. The moon shone brightly, and the white pebbles in front of the house glittered like real silver pennies. Hansel bent down and filled his coat’s little pocket with as many as he could fit. Then he returned and said to Grethel, “Take comfort, dear little sister, and sleep peacefully. God will not abandon us.” He lay down in bed again. At daybreak, before the sun had risen, the woman woke them. “Get up, you lazy children! We’re going into the forest to fetch wood.” She gave each a small piece of bread. “That’s for your midday meal,” she said. “Don’t eat it before then, because you’ll get nothing else.” Grethel put the bread under her apron, since Hansel had stones in his pocket. They all set off towards the forest. After a short walk, Hansel stopped and looked back at the house, and kept doing so. “Hansel,” his father said, “what are you looking at, and why are you hanging behind? Pay attention and remember how to use your legs.” “Oh, Father,” Hansel said, “I’m looking at my little white cat on the roof. It wants to say goodbye to me.” “Fool,” his father’s wife said, “that isn’t your little cat. It’s the morning sun shining on the chimneys.” But Hansel had not been looking at the cat. He had been dropping white pebbles from his pocket onto the road, one after another.

When they reached the middle of the forest, their father said, “Now, children, pile up some wood. I’ll light a fire so you won’t be cold.” Hansel and Grethel gathered brushwood into a heap as high as a small hill. It was lit, and when the flames burned high, the woman said, “Now lie down by the fire and rest. We’re going into the forest to cut wood. When we’re finished, we’ll come back for you.”

Hansel and Grethel sat by the fire. At noon, they each ate a little bread. They heard what sounded like an axe striking wood and believed their father was nearby. But it was not an axe. He had tied a branch to a withered tree, and the wind was blowing it back and forth. After sitting so long, the children’s eyes closed with tiredness, and they fell fast asleep. When they finally woke, it was already dark. Grethel began to cry. “How will we get out of the forest now?” she asked. But Hansel comforted her. “Wait a little until the moon rises,” he said. “Then we’ll soon find the way.” When the full moon rose, he took his little sister’s hand and followed the pebbles, shining like newly minted silver coins and showing them the path.

They walked all night and reached their father’s house again at daybreak. They knocked. When the woman opened the door and saw Hansel and Grethel, she said, “You naughty children! Why did you sleep so long in the forest? We thought you were never coming back!” Their father, however, was overjoyed. Leaving them alone had broken his heart.

Not long afterwards, there was another great shortage everywhere. At night, the children heard their mother saying to their father, “Everything has been eaten again. We have half a loaf left, and after that there’s nothing. The children must go. We’ll take them farther into the wood so they cannot find their way back. There’s no other way to save ourselves.” The man’s heart was heavy. “It would be better to share your last mouthful with your children,” he thought. But the woman would not listen to anything he said. She scolded and reproached him. Someone who says A must also say B: since he had given in the first time, he had to give in again.

The children were still awake and had heard everything. Once the grown-ups were asleep, Hansel got up again, meaning to collect pebbles as before. But the woman had locked the door, and he could not get out. Even so, he comforted his little sister. “Don’t cry, Grethel,” he said. “Go to sleep peacefully. The good God will help us.”

Early the next morning, the woman came and took them out of bed. They were given their bread, an even smaller piece than before. On the way to the forest, Hansel crumbled his in his pocket, often stopping to drop a little on the ground. “Hansel, why do you keep stopping and looking around?” his father asked. “Keep going.” “I’m looking back at my little pigeon on the roof,” Hansel answered. “It wants to say goodbye.” “Simpleton!” the woman said. “That isn’t your little pigeon. It’s the morning sun shining on the chimney.” But little by little, Hansel dropped all his crumbs onto the path.

The woman led them still deeper into the forest, to a place they had never been in their lives. Another great fire was made. “Sit there, children,” their mother said. “When you’re tired, you can sleep a little. We’re going into the forest to cut wood. This evening, when we’ve finished, we’ll come for you.” At noon, Grethel shared her bread with Hansel, who had scattered his along the way. Then they fell asleep. Evening came and went, but no one came for the poor children. They did not wake until it was dark. Hansel comforted his little sister. “Just wait until the moon rises, Grethel,” he said. “Then we’ll see the breadcrumbs I scattered. They’ll show us the way home.” When the moon appeared, they set out, but found no crumbs. The many thousands of birds that fly through the woods and fields had eaten them all. “We’ll soon find the way,” Hansel told Grethel, but they did not. They walked all night and all the next day, from morning until evening, without escaping the forest. They were very hungry, with nothing to eat except two or three berries growing on the ground. At last they were so tired that their legs could carry them no farther. They lay beneath a tree and fell asleep.

It was now the third morning since they had left their father’s house. They began walking again but only went deeper into the forest. Without help soon, they would die of hunger and exhaustion. At midday they saw a beautiful snow-white bird sitting on a branch. It sang so sweetly that they stopped to listen. When its song ended, it spread its wings and flew ahead of them. They followed until they reached a little house, and the bird landed on its roof. Close up, they saw that the house was built of bread and roofed with cakes, while its windows were clear sugar. “We’ll get to work on that and have a good meal,” Hansel said. “I’ll eat some roof, and you can eat some window, Grethel. It will taste sweet.” Hansel reached up and broke off a little roof to taste. Grethel leaned against a window and nibbled its panes. Then a soft voice called from inside:

“Nibble, nibble, gnaw,
Who is nibbling at my little house?”
The children answered:

“The wind, the wind,
The wind from heaven,”

and went on eating without a care. Hansel thought the roof tasted very good and pulled off a great piece. Grethel pushed out an entire round windowpane, sat down and enjoyed eating it. Suddenly the door opened. A very, very old woman, leaning on crutches, came creeping out. Hansel and Grethel were so frightened that they dropped what they were holding. But the old woman nodded. “Oh, you dear children, who brought you here?” she said. “Come in and stay with me. No harm will come to you.” She took them both by the hand and led them inside. Good food was set before them: milk and pancakes with sugar, apples and nuts. Afterwards, clean white linen was spread on two pretty little beds. Hansel and Grethel lay down and thought they were in heaven.

The old woman had only pretended to be kind. She was really a wicked witch who lay in wait for children. She had built the little bread house only to lure them there. When a child fell into her power, she killed, cooked and ate it, and that was a feast day for her. Witches have red eyes and cannot see far, but they have a sharp sense of smell, like animals, and know when people come near. When Hansel and Grethel approached her home, she laughed maliciously. “I’ve got them!” she said mockingly. “They won’t escape me again.” Early the next morning, before the children woke, she was already up. Seeing them asleep, so pretty with their plump red cheeks, she muttered, “What a delicious mouthful!” She seized Hansel with her shrivelled hand, carried him to a small stable, and locked him behind a barred door. He could scream all he liked; it was no use. Then she went to Grethel, shook her awake, and cried, “Get up, lazy thing! Fetch water and cook something good for your brother. He’s in the stable outside and must be fattened. When he is fat, I’ll eat him.” Grethel began to weep bitterly, but it was no use. She had to obey the wicked witch.

Now the best food was cooked for poor Hansel, while Grethel got only crab shells. Every morning, the old woman crept to the stable. “Hansel, put out your finger,” she called, “so I can feel whether you’ll soon be fat.” But Hansel held out a little bone. The old woman’s eyes were dim; she could not see it and thought it was his finger. She was astonished that she could not fatten him. After four weeks, when Hansel was still thin, she lost patience and would wait no longer. “Here, Grethel!” she called. “Be quick and bring water. Fat or thin, tomorrow I’ll kill Hansel and cook him.” Oh, how the poor little sister wept as she fetched the water, and how the tears ran down her cheeks! “Dear God, please help us!” she cried. “If only the wild animals in the forest had eaten us! At least we would have died together.” “Keep your noise to yourself,” the old woman said. “None of that will help you.”

Early the next morning, Grethel had to go out, hang up the cauldron of water, and light the fire. “We’ll bake first,” the old woman said. “I’ve already heated the oven and kneaded the dough.” She pushed poor Grethel towards the oven, where flames were already darting out. “Crawl inside,” the witch said, “and see whether it’s hot enough, so we can put the bread in and shut it inside.” Once Grethel was inside, she meant to close the oven and bake her, then eat her too. But Grethel understood what she intended. “I don’t know how to do it,” she said. “How do you get in?” “Silly goose,” the old woman said. “The door is big enough. Look, I can get in myself!” She crept up and put her head inside. Grethel gave her a push that sent her far into the oven, shut the iron door and slid the bolt. Oh, how horribly the witch howled! But Grethel ran away, and the godless witch burned miserably to death.

Grethel ran like lightning to Hansel, opened his little stable, and cried, “Hansel, we’re saved! The old witch is dead!” Hansel sprang out like a bird from its cage when the door is opened. How they rejoiced, hugged, danced and kissed each other! Since they no longer had to fear her, they went into the witch’s house. In every corner stood chests full of pearls and jewels. “These are much better than pebbles!” Hansel said, filling his pockets with everything they would hold. “I’ll take something home too,” Grethel said, filling her apron. “But now we must go,” Hansel said, “and get out of the witch’s forest.”

After walking for two hours, they reached a great stretch of water. “We can’t cross,” Hansel said. “I see no plank or bridge.” “And there’s no boat crossing either,” Grethel answered. “But a white duck is swimming there. If I ask her, she’ll help us across.” Then she called:

“Little duck, little duck, can you see?
Hansel and Grethel are waiting for you.
There is no plank or bridge in sight;
Carry us across on your back so white.”

The duck came to them. Hansel sat on her back and told his sister to sit beside him. “No,” Grethel said. “That would be too heavy for the little duck. She must take us across one at a time.” The good little duck did so. Once safely across, the children walked for a little while, and the forest began to look more and more familiar. At last they saw their father’s house in the distance. They began running, rushed into the sitting room, and threw themselves into his arms. He had not known one happy hour since leaving them in the forest. The woman, however, was dead. Grethel emptied her apron until pearls and precious stones rolled around the room. Hansel added handful after handful from his pocket. All their worries were over, and they lived together in perfect happiness. My tale is done. There runs a mouse—whoever catches it can make a big fur cap from it.
